UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

         PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                  )             Docket No. ER26-3515-000


                           LIMITED PROTEST AND COMMENTS OF
                             FIRSTENERGY SERVICE COMPANY

        Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), 1 FirstEnergy Service Company, as agent for

its affiliates (“FirstEnergy”), 2 respectfully submits this Limited Protest and Comments in response

to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) August 13, 2026 filing, proposing to establish an

Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) mechanism. 3

        In the Statement of Principles Regarding PJM (“Statement of Principles”), the National

Energy Dominance Council and 13 of the Governors of the PJM States joined together and

identified that there would be a class of new data centers that have not self-procured capacity or

agreed to be curtailable. 4 Under the Statement of Principles, this class of new data centers was to

be excluded from PJM’s procurement of new Capacity Resources. PJM’s IRAS Proposal purports

to outline how service is to be provided at the wholesale level to this class of data centers; the

headline being that these new data centers either must bring their own new capacity (“BYONC”)

or be curtailable.



1
        18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
        FirstEnergy’s affiliates include Ohio Edison Company, The Cleveland Electric Illuminating Company, The
Toledo Edison Company, FirstEnergy Pennsylvania Electric Company, Jersey Central Power & Light Company,
Monongahela Power Company, and The Potomac Edison Company.
3
         Docket No. ER26-3515, PJM, Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load
Registry to Address System Reliability (“PJM IRAS Proposal”).
4
         Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, 1st and                 3rd    bullets   (1/16/26),   available
https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm.
          FirstEnergy agrees that new data centers that are not included within the scope of a PJM

capacity procurement must either bring their own new capacity or be curtailable. Unfortunately,

fundamental elements of PJM’s IRAS Proposal are fatally flawed and as a result these elements

cannot be approved consistent with section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”).

         Section 205 of the FPA provides that the Commission can accept PJM’s RPM proposal

only if it is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. 5 The filing utility—

PJM—bears the burden of proof to demonstrate its proposal meets these FPA requirements. 6 The

Commission may accept PJM’s proposal only if there is sufficient evidence in the record to show

PJM has carried its section 205 burden of proof. 7 The Commission will reject any proposal that

falls outside the zone of reasonableness—i.e., does not result in just and reasonable rates in

accordance with section 205. 8 Moreover, even if a rate falls within the zone of reasonableness, it

may nevertheless violate section 205 due to being unduly discriminatory or preferential. 9

         In these comments, FirstEnergy demonstrates that PJM’s IRAS Proposal does not meet the

FPA section 205 “just and reasonable” standard because:

    1. PJM unlawfully is attempting to set retail rates by proposing that new data centers that are
       to be curtailable under the IRAS Proposal are to be paid to curtail;
    2. PJM is discriminating against new generation that aligns itself with a new data center by
       requiring such new generation to participate in the RPM auctions for 10 years;

         3. PJM fails to align the timing of its IRAS Proposal with applicable Commission guidance;
           and
        4. Various of the implementing details are beyond the scope of the Statement of Principles
           and are unnecessary and/or inconsistent with other elements of the Commission’s
           developing data center policies and directives, and thus must be dropped from PJM’s
           eventual compliance filing.
            LIMITED PROTEST AND COMMENTS

I.      PJM is unlawfully attempting to set retail rates by proposing that new data centers that
        are to be curtailable under the IRAS Proposal are to be paid to curtail.

            As the Commission is aware, its ratemaking jurisdiction is limited to interstate transmission

     and wholesale power sales. 10 States regulate retail rates for retail customers. And new data centers

  are retail customers.

            These broad principles notwithstanding, PJM has filed a tariff that calls for retail payments

  to be made when new data centers are curtailed. 11 PJM even goes so far as to propose a retail rate

     that is to be paid to the curtailing data center; although PJM leaves final determination of the

     payment amount in the hands of the jurisdictional state. 12

            There is no basis under federal law for PJM to propose this rate. PJM’s IRAS Proposal is

     careful to exclude curtailable new data centers from its “Reliability Pricing Model” capacity

     procurement. 13 In fact, such loads are not participating directly in any PJM power market. This

     is because they are retail loads. It is true that Load-Serving Entities may buy power at wholesale

     for resale for end-use consumption by a new data center. But this does not mean that a curtailable

     new data center is participating directly in PJM’s power markets. As such, these loads do not




  10
            16 U.S.C. §§ 824, 824d, 824e.
  11
            PJM IRAS Proposal, Filing Letter, pp. 101, et seq., and the proposed tariff amendments described therein.
  12
            Id., p. 102.
  13
            Id., p. 55.



                                                            3
 resemble “demand response” as that product is defined in the PJM tariffs or in applicable state

retail programs.

       There is no policy guidance that calls PJM to create a Commission-jurisdictional

compensation mechanism for new data center loads that are to be curtailable. As noted above, the

Statement of Principles contemplates that certain new data centers will be curtailable. But the

Statement of Principles does not call for PJM to create a compensation mechanism to pay for such

resources during periods of curtailment. And PJM points to no other policy guidance that compels

creation of a rate that provides payments to the new data centers – that are retail customers – that

are required to curtail during periods of capacity shortfalls.

       The unlawful nature of PJM’s proposal is demonstrated by PJM’s implicit recognition that

the jurisdictional state authority must set the amount of the final payment. 14 That PJM is calling

for states and LSEs to identify the other retail customers that are to fund such payments again

reflects the fact that PJM’s proposal is about retail rates, even if it is dressed up as purported

amendments to a Commission-jurisdictional tariff.

       The tariff amendments that are embodied in PJM’s IRAS Proposal do not reflect the

jurisdictional boundary between the Commission and the states. Indeed, the states must retain

control over determining the need for new power generation facilities, the economic feasibility of

such facilities, and the rates and services to be provided by suppliers of the same. 15 The

Commission’s role is limited to regulating wholesale power sales. 16 That is, the Commission can

regulate a wholesale power market, as it does with PJM and the other RTOs. But the Commission

cannot direct a utility to build new generation, and it cannot establish retail rate recovery that can


14
       PJM IRAS Proposal, Filing Letter, p. 104.
15
       See, e.g., Hughes v Talen, 136 S.Ct. 1288 at 1292 (US 2016).
16
       16 U.S.C. 824(b)(1).



                                                      4
       pay for new generation. And, just as FERC cannot establish a retail rate to pay for new generation,

      FERC cannot establish a retail rate that pays a new data center to curtail when there is not sufficient

      generation capacity available to serve that customer. These functions are reserved for the states.

             Moreover, beyond the jurisdictional issues, the concept of compensating new large loads

      to curtail in the IRAS Proposal is deficient from a policy perspective and is contrary to the intent

      of the Statement of Principles which is to protect customers from the costs associated with

      integrating large loads. However, the IRAS Proposal, as designed, will in fact unjustly raise costs

      to retail customers with no corresponding benefits, and rewards imprudent owners of new large

      load facilities for their failure to procure new capacity to serve their own load. PJM attempts to

      smooth over this dynamic by pointing to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge as a mechanism to avoid

      passing costs associated with the IRAS Proposal on to retail customers. The Ratepayer Protection

      Pledge, however, is not a binding legal document and would not prevent new large loads from

      seeking compensation pursuant to the IRAS Proposal mechanisms.

             Thus, for these reasons, the Commission must reject PJM’s attempt to create a retail rate

  as part of the IRAS Proposal.

II.          The IRAS Proposal includes no justification for requiring BYONC generation
             resources to participate in RPM for 10 years, and the Commission should require
             PJM to drop this requirement.

             There is no basis for PJM to create a minimum 10-year term for participation in the

  annual RPM auction for new BYONC resources. 17 Although it is not spelled out, if a data center

      aligns itself with a new generation resource, it is reasonable to assume that the data center has

      signed a contract that is the basis for financing the new resources. That is, the funding for a new




      17
             PJM IRAS Proposal, Filing Letter, p. 55 and et seq. (and the tariff amendments described therein).



                                                             5
        BYONC generation resource should be understood to come from the commercial arrangements

       between the new data center and the generation resource.

              It is axiomatic that marginal-price market models do not pay for new capital investment

       in high cost-of-capital fields; an outcome that is reflected by the fact that marginal-price design

    RPM has brought very little significant new dispatchable generation in PJM. The new data

    center, and not PJM’s RPM program, will be funding the capital investment in the new resource.

    As such, there is no need, or reason, to compel the new generation resources to be in the RPM

    auction for 10 years.

III.          PJM is discriminating against new generation that aligns itself with a new data
              center by proscribing the opportunity for that resource to serve as a Fixed Resource
              Requirement generator.

              PJM proposes that new BYONC resources must participate in RPM. 18 That is, PJM is

       forcing new Capacity Resources that are aligned with new data centers into the RPM market.

              This is unduly discriminatory and preferential as it treats data centers and data center-

       aligned new resources differently from new loads and generation that otherwise have the option to

       opt into a full or partial Fixed Resource Requirement (FRR).

              Section B of Schedule 8.1 of the PJM Reliability Assurance Agreement (RAA) sets forth

       the terms under which a certain load may “opt out” of the RPM program by demonstrating that it

       is eligible for the FRR program. 19 An eligible LSE must demonstrate that all or part of its load

       falls within the RAA’s FRR Service Area definition (capable of being metered separately from

       other load), and that it has procured eligible Capacity Resources to cover that load and the FRR-

       defined associated resource adequacy reserve requirement. Importantly, because they are in an



       18
              PJM IRAS Proposal, Filing Letter, p. 55 and et seq. (and the tariff amendments described therein).
       19
              PJM Reliability Assurance Agreement, Schedule 8.1, B.



                                                              6
       FRR “alternative,” eligible loads, and the associated generation, are not subject to the annual RPM

      auction.

               FirstEnergy agrees with PJM that new data centers can be established as a new class of

      customers that are subject to different capacity rules than other loads. 20 However, there is no basis

   to obligate a new data center, and the new generation resources that have been procured to supply

   that data center, to participate in the annual RPM auctions. On the contrary, PJM’s IRAS proposal

   contemplates that new data centers with associated new Capacity Resources in existing FRR areas

   will be excluded from the RPM auction. But PJM does not afford the opportunity for a new load

   with associated new generation that is not in an existing FRR area to take advantage of the FRR

   opportunity.

               If new data centers and associated new Capacity Resources in existing FRR areas are

   exempted from the RPM auction, then there is no basis to force new Capacity Resources that are

   not in an existing FRR area to participate in the RPM auction. On the contrary, given the vagaries

      of the RPM construct, prudent data center developers and associated developers of generation

      resources have every reason to demand that they be allowed to take advantage of the FRR

      alternative, and be afforded the opportunity to do so. Requiring participation in the RPM auction,

      as PJM so proposes, is unduly discriminatory and preferential. 21

IV.            PJM fails to align the timing of the IRAS Proposal with applicable Commission
               guidance.

               The Statement of Principles provides policy guidance about the timing of the programs

   contemplated therein. Specifically, the Statement of Principles provides that PJM is to conduct a

              16 U.S.C. § 824d(a)-(b); see also Ala. Elec. Coop, Inc. v. FERC, 684 F.2d at 27 (citing U.S. v. Cent. Ill. R.R.,
      263 U.S. at 524).



                                                                 7
 Reliability Backstop [Procurement] to procure new Capacity Resources for new data centers that

have not self-procured or agreed to be curtailable. 22 Importantly, the policy guidance issued to

PJM is to make changes for “new” data centers. Existing data centers implicitly are grandfathered.

       PJM’s IRAS Proposal purports to apply to new data centers that go into service after June

1, 2027. 23 However, there could be a difference between “new” data centers and data centers that

go into service after June 1, 2027. Specifically, it is possible that a developer of a data center may

have signed a construction agreement for new transmission network facilities before January 16,

2026 and that due to the process of construction the data center may not go into service until after

June 1, 2027. This customer is not “new” within the scope of the Statement of Principles and

should be grandfathered. Importantly, the fact that these customers are not “new” within the

contemplated scope of the agreement could mean that attempting to apply the IRAS Proposal to

them could violate the filed rate doctrine because to do so would undermine preexisting

commercial relationships by attempting to allocate capacity market outcomes to data centers who

possibly have already signed FERC-jurisdictional contracts based on a pre-IRAS Proposal

understanding of the market.

       Relevant here is that PJM makes no effort to demonstrate that its proposal, at least for the

customers described in the prior paragraph, is consistent with relevant Commission guidance.

Specifically, in its June 18, 2026 Order to Show Cause, the Commission identified that certain

data centers were, as of the date of the Order, working with transmission owners and other relevant

entities to take service from the transmission system. 24 The Commission further identified that

there is a need to protect existing commercial arrangements, that stakeholders needed to ensure

      minimal disruption to existing commercial arrangements, and that stakeholders were to

     thoughtfully develop proposals to establish a reasonable amount of time to finalize agreements

     that are nearing completion as of the date when tariff amendments were filed for Commission

     approval. 25

             PJM’s “one size fits all” IRAS Proposal does not protect against disruption to existing

     commercial arrangements, and it makes no effort to establish a reasonable time to finalize

     agreements that are nearing completion as of the date when the IRAS Proposal was filed. That is,

     PJM failed to align the timing of the IRAS Proposal with the Commission’s guidance about

     existing and nearly final commercial arrangements. As such, the Commission should reject PJM’s

     “one size fits all” date of “enters service after June 1, 2027,” and instead direct PJM to develop an

     IRAS Proposal effective date that does not disrupt existing commercial arrangements and that

     provides sufficient notice so that stakeholders can complete contracting processes that are “in

     flight” as to the date of PJM’s future compliance filing.

V.           Various of the implementing details are beyond the scope of the Statement of
             Principles and are unnecessary and/or inconsistent with other elements of the
             Commission’s developing data center policies and directives, and thus must be
             dropped from PJM’s eventual compliance filing.

             Certain aspects of PJM’s IRAS Proposal are not consistent with the express or implied

 policy guidance that is provided in the Statement of Principles or other applicable Commission

     guidance. As such, these details do not clear the “just and reasonable” legal standard for evaluating

     tariff amendments. As outlined in the following sections, the Commission should require PJM to

 address these instances by submitting further amendments in order to bring these instances into

 harmony with the Statement of Principles and the other applicable Commission guidance.




     25
             Id.

            A. The definition of “Large Load” should be adjusted, either to take the minimum
              megawatt threshold to 200 MW, or to limit the definition to new data centers.

       As relevant here, PJM proposes to define Large Loads as an end-use customer that has a

cumulative peak of 50MW or greater. 26 This definition will capture new data centers. But it will

also capture small and medium-sized manufacturing facilities.

       The scope of the Statement of Principles document, which is the policy guidance that

should control for review of PJM’s IRAS proposal, is limited to new data centers. 27 And for good

cause. It is true that similar energy infrastructure must be constructed without regard to whether

the new facility is a data center or a manufacturing facility. But that is where the similarity ends.

Manufacturing facilities generate numerous upstream, local and downstream investment and jobs;

whereas data centers do not. That is, manufacturing facilities generate significant upstream, local

and downstream benefits for workers, their communities, and the states that comprise PJM;

whereas the economic benefits of data centers are different and more limited.

       There are material differences between a new data center and a manufacturing facility.

First, a new data center will generate many jobs during initial construction; but very few full-time

jobs post construction, whereas a new manufacturing facility will generate many permanent full-

time jobs. Next, once it is up and running, the new data center will consume enormous amounts

of energy, and that’s it. In contrast, a new manufacturing facility will consume raw and somewhat

processed materials; the extraction/processing/supply of such also will generate many full-time

jobs. Importantly, each full-time job that is supported directly or indirectly by a manufacturing

facility will support a family. And families own homes, pay taxes, and participate in communities.




26
       PJM IRAS Proposal, Filing Letter, p. 31, and the proposed tariff amendments described therein.
27
       Statement of Principles, 3rd bullet.



                                                      10
          The differences are not limited to jobs. For example, data centers likely can be curtailed

on short notice with little consequence. But there are consequences for curtailing manufacturing

facilities on short notice, including at least: upstream and downstream supply chain disruption;

work stoppages for affected workers; lost inventory that is stranded in the manufacturing process;

damage to manufacturing equipment; and cleaning and restarting of manufacturing equipment.

         PJM is unable to demonstrate that it clears the FPA section 205 hurdle for including

manufacturing facilities within the scope of the IRAS proposal. This is because it is unjust and

unreasonable to include manufacturing facilities within scope. Manufacturing facilities are not

like data centers, and they also are not within the scope of the Statement of Principles guidance.

And imposing what amounts to a “tax” on future operations will likely have the unintended

consequence of driving investment and jobs out of PJM and into regions of the country that are

more welcoming; that is, including manufacturing facilities within the scope of the IRAS proposal

is unduly discriminatory and preferential 28 against manufacturing facilities that are attempting to

locate or expand in PJM as compared to other regions. As such, the Commission should direct

PJM to either raise the MW threshold for IRAS applicability (to 200 MW) or refine the Large Load

definition to limit the rule to new data centers.

             B. The criteria for the Large Load registry must match the criteria that are to be set
                forth in the pro forma agreement that is described in the Commission’s June 18,
                2026 Order to Show Cause.

         The Commission’s June 18, 2026 Order to Show Cause included a preliminary finding that

PJM’s tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks a pro forma agreement that

itemizes the terms and requirements under which a new data center would take transmission

 service. 29 Importantly, PJM and the Transmission Owners are to submit a compliance filing that,

among other things, provides the pro forma agreement anticipated in the Order to Show Cause. 30

       In the IRAS Proposal, PJM outlines the data that data centers must submit to be included

in a contemplated “Registry.” 31 FirstEnergy does not object to many of these criteria, but notes

that the criteria should not be finalized until the pro forma agreement and “registry” that are

contemplated in the Order to Show Cause are finalized.

           C. PJM should clarify that the Data Center, and not the Load-Serving Entity, is
              responsible for certain compliance obligations.

       PJM’s IRAS Proposal is filled with terms, requirements, obligations, and conditions that

attach to data centers under the IRAS. But, from time to time, PJM attempts to place some of these

conditions on Load-Serving Entities. For example, the IRAS Proposal provides that LSEs must

bring new capacity or be subject to load reductions. 32

       PJM, no doubt, intended confusion concerning this aspect of the IRAS Proposal. However,

PJM’s language is confusing. Sometimes the terms, requirements, obligations, and conditions are

described as pertaining to the new data center. And, as noted, at other times, PJM suggests that

they pertain to the LSE.

       Assuming that at some future time some form of PJM’s IRAS Proposal is approved, the

Commission can remedy this deficiency by directing PJM to clarify which entity holds the

obligations. For example, PJM could create new classes of LSEs and Electric Distribution

            D. PJM should clarify that “Energy Resources” can be “new” Capacity Resources for
               purposes of evaluating a Data Center’s compliance with the proposed Bring Your
               Own New Capacity option for removal from IRAS.

        PJM proposes that new data centers can remove themselves – in whole or part – from the

IRAS if the new data center brings new capacity. PJM goes on, however, to clarify that a new

Capacity Resource cannot be existing generation that is “repackaged.” 33

        It is clear that PJM is attempting to ensure that existing Capacity Resources are not

removed from the Reliability Pricing Model markets and then paired with a new data center so that

the new data center can be removed from the IRAS. However, there is a class of generating

resources that currently are not Capacity Resources.                  Specifically, PJM’s Open Access

Transmission Tariff defines an “Energy Resource” as a Generating Facility that is not a Capacity

Resource. 34 Energy Resources do not have RPM obligations, and receive no RPM revenues.

Instead, Energy Resources typically limit their power market participation to selling energy and

ancillary services into PJM’s day-ahead and real-time markets. Because such resources are not

committed to the RPM market, they are not Capacity Resources.

        The Commission should direct PJM to allow Energy Resources to qualify as “new

capacity” for purposes of evaluating whether a data center can be removed from IRAS. There is

no basis to exclude Energy Resources. Excluding such resources would be unduly discriminatory

 and preferential 35 in that it would prohibit Energy Resources from entering the capacity market as

supply for the new data centers that wish to bring their own new capacity.

             E. There is no justification for dropping the IRAS rules if PJM has sufficient capacity
                to meet the RPM requirement for three consecutive years.

         PJM proposes that the IRAS rules will not apply if PJM has sufficient capacity to meet the

RPM requirement for three consecutive years. 36                     This proposal, however, is unjust and

unreasonable as it would allow data center loads that are “new” after the termination of the IRAS

rules to enter with the expectation of firm capacity supply. There is no basis to expect that such

firm supply will exist. PJM itself admits that its current capacity resource shortfall is at least 6,831

MW. 37 And the Statement of Principles notes that PJM must procure new Capacity Resources to

serve new data centers that do not self-supply or agree to be curtailable. 38 The Statement of

Principles does not authorize PJM to allow new data centers to enter the market when there is not

sufficient supply. And new data centers now range from hundreds to more than a thousand

megawatts of demand. 39 This is not the incremental load growth for which the RPM construct was

designed. The mere fact that the RPM market has cleared for three consecutive years does not

mean that there is enough “headroom” to absorb hundreds or possibly thousands of new megawatts

of new load. Moreover, this proposal is unjust and unreasonable in that it allows “new” data

centers that enter the market after termination of the IRAS rules to ride on the capacity that is being

             F. There is no justification for requiring BYONC generation resources to participate
                in RPM for 10 years, and the Commission should require PJM to drop this
                requirement.

         There is no basis for PJM to create a minimum 10-year term for participation in the annual

RPM auction for new BYONC resources. 41 Although it is not spelled out, as the impetus for

funding a new BYONC resource should be understood to come from the commercial arrangements

between the new data center and the generation resource. It is axiomatic that marginal-price

markets models do not pay for new capital investment in high cost-of-capital fields; an outcome

that is reflected by the fact that marginal-price design RPM has brought very little significant new

dispatchable generation in PJM. The new data center, and not PJM’s RPM program, will be

funding the capital investment in the new resource. If there is to be a minimum term, it should be

set at a minimum term for the new data center to be removed from the IRAS program, and not on

the basis that the data center brought new generation.

             G. PJM must provide additional clarification regarding the new data centers that
                qualify for reduced IRAS due to being allocated a share of the Reliability Backstop
                Procurement megawatts.

         PJM proposes that a new data center that could be subject to the IRAS can have its IRAS

obligations reduced or eliminated by virtue of being allocated a share of the new Capacity

Resources that are to be procured through PJM’s proposed “Reliability Backstop Procurement”

(RBP). 42 Given, however, that the RBP capacity is to be allocated to data center loads that were

             H. IRAS obligations must be allocated to data centers that did not agree to be
                curtailable.

         PJM proposes to reallocate IRAS curtailment obligations annually. 45                         That is, PJM

proposes to reallocate curtailment obligations annually based on the level of the capacity shortfall

for a given region.         As capacity shortfalls ebb and flow, PJM will reallocate curtailment

obligations. The proposal is unduly discriminatory and preferential as it could allow new data

centers that did not bring their own generation to avoid curtailment based on market activity of

other market participants.

         The Statement of Principles, which is the policy guidance that should control for review of

PJM’s IRAS proposal, provides that new data centers either must participate in the RBP, or bring

their own generation, or agree to be curtailable. 46 It does not allow a data center to exit a

curtailment obligation because, through the activity of some other market participant, the region

in which the data center is not located no longer is net-short of capacity. And, under PJM’s

proposal, the “net short” conditions will change because either other loads exited the region or

because unaffiliated new Capacity Resources entered the region.
